1220.text: If maximum energy is stored in capacitor at $t=0$, then find the time after which current in the circuit will be maximum
1220.sol:
In $L-C$ oscillations, total time in one complete cycle is, $T=2 \pi \sqrt{L C} \begin{aligned} & T=2 \pi \sqrt{25 \times 10^{-3} \times 10 \times 10^{-6}} \\ & \Rightarrow T=2 \pi \sqrt{25 \times 10^{-8}} \\ & =\pi \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{sec}\end{aligned}$
After time $T / 4$ capacitor is fully discharged and current in circuit will be maximum, then $\frac{T}{4}=\frac{\pi \times 10^{-3}}{4}=\frac{\pi}{4} \mathrm{~ms}$

options: If both assertion and reason are true and reason is the correct explanation of assertion
If both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion

2093.sol: The female secondary sexual characters are developed by estrogens. Estrogens are steroid hormones secreted by growing ovarian follicles. It includes estradiol, estriol and estrone. Gonadotrophic hormones (LH and FSH) are secreted by the anterior lobe of pituitary gland. $\mathrm{LH}$ is responsible for ovulation and transforms graafian follicle into corpus luteum and FSH stimulates spermatogenesis and maturation of graafian follicle and secretion of estrogen in ovaries.

6907.subject: Mathematics
6907.text: The Locus of centers of the circles, possessing the same area and having $3x - 4y + 4 = 0$ and $6x - 8y - 7 = 0$ as their common tangent, is
6907.sol:
Given,

$3x - 4y + 4 = 0$ and $6x - 8y - 7 = 0$ are common tangent,

Now the given lines are parallel tangents to a circle,

So, the diameter of the circle is equal to the distance between these lines,

So that the required radius is

$\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{4 + \dfrac{7}{2}}{\sqrt{9 + 16}} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{15}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{5} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

The center of the circle lies on the line parallel to the given lines at a distance of $\dfrac{3}{4}$ from each of them.

So let the equation passing from center be $3x - 4y + k = 0 ⋯ \left(1\right)$

Then by distance between two parallel line formula we get, $\dfrac{k - 4}{\sqrt{9 + 16}} = \pm \dfrac{3}{4} ⇒ k = 4 \pm \left(\dfrac{15}{4}\right) ⇒ k = \dfrac{1}{4}$ or $\dfrac{31}{4}$

For $k = \dfrac{1}{4}$, distance of $\left(1\right)$ from the other line is also $\dfrac{3}{4}$.

Thus the center lies on the line $3x - 4y + \dfrac{1}{4} = 0$

 $⇒ 12x - 16y + 1 = 0$

7030.sol:
Equation of polar of point \(P(2,3)\) with respect to the circle \(x²+y²-2 x-2 y+1=0\) is
$\begin{aligned}$& T=0 \Rightarrow 2 x+3 y-(x+2)-(y+3)+1=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad x+2 y-4=0 \quad \ldots (i)
\end{aligned}\)
End equation of $line joining of points \(P(2,3)\) and centre of the given circle \(C(1,1)\) is
\(y-1=\frac{2}{1}($x-1) \Rightarrow 2 x-y-1=0 \quad \ldots (ii)\)
\(\because\) Inverse point of $\(P\) with respect to the given circle is point of intersection of polar Eq. (i) and line CP, Eq. (ii), so coordinate of the inverse point is
\(Q\left(\frac{6}{5}, \frac{7}{5}\right) \text{. }$
Now, equation of polar of point \(Q$\left(\frac{6}{5}, \frac{7}{5}\right)$ with respect to given circle is
$\begin{aligned}$& $\frac{6}{5}$x+$\frac{7}{5}$y-$\left(x+$\frac{6}{5}\right)-\left(y+$\frac{7}{5}\right)+$1=0 \\
\Rightarrow \quad & x+2 y-8=0 \quad \ldots (iii)
\end{aligned}\)
\(\therefore\) Required distance between polars (i) and $(iii) is
\(\frac{4}{\sqrt{1+4}}=\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}}$
Hence, option (b) is correct.

12090.text: Given that lines \(L_1: y=m_a x, L_2: y=m_b x\) and \(L_3: y=m_c x\) make equal intercepts on the line \(x+y=1\), then
12090.sol:
Since, the point of intersecting of given lines \(L_1: y=m_a x, L_2: y=m_b x\) and \(L_3: y=m_c x\) with line \(x+y=1\) are
$\begin{aligned}
& A\left(\frac{1}{1+m_a}, \frac{m a}{1+m_a}\right), B\left(\frac{1}{1+m_b}, \frac{m_b}{1+m_b}\right) \text{$ and $} \\
& C\left(\frac{1}{1+m_c}, \frac{m_c}{1+m_c}\right) \text{ respectively. }
\end{aligned}\)
It is given that,
\(A B=B C \Rightarrow A B^2=B C^2\)
\(\begin{gathered}
\Rightarrow\left(\frac{1}{1+m_a}-\frac{1}{1+m_b}\right)^2+\left(\frac{m_a}{1+m_a}-\frac{m_b}{1+m_b}\right)^2 \\
=\left(\frac{1}{1+m_b}-\frac{1}{1+m_c}\right)^2+\left(\frac{m_b}{1+m_b}-\frac{m_c}{1+m_c}\right)^2 \\
\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\left(m_b-m_a\right)^2}{\left(1+m_a\right)^2\left(1+m_b\right)^2}+\frac{\left(m_a-m_b\right)^2}{\left(1+m_a\right)^2\left(1+m_b\right)^2} \\
=\frac{\left(m_c-m_b\right)^2}{\left(1+m_b\right)^2\left(1+m_c\right)^2}+\frac{\left(m_b-m_c\right)^2}{\left(1+m_b\right)^2\left(1+m_c\right)^2} \\
\Rightarrow \quad 2 \frac{\left(m_a-m_b\right)^2}{\left(1+m_a\right)^2\left(1+m_b\right)^2}=2 \frac{\left(m_b-m_c\right)^2}{\left(1+m_b\right)^2\left(1+m_c\right)^2} \\
\Rightarrow \quad\left(m_a-m_b\right)\left(1+m_c\right)=\left(m_b-m_c\right)\left(1+m_a\right) \\
\Rightarrow \quad\left[\left(1+m_a\right)-\left(1+m_b\right)\right]\left(1+m_c\right) =\left[\left(1+m_b\right)-\left(1+m_c\right)\right]\left(1+m_a\right) \\
\Rightarrow \quad 2\left(1+m_a\right)\left(1+m_c\right)=\left(1+m_b\right)\left(1+m_c+1+m_a\right) \\
\Rightarrow \quad 2\left(1+m_a\right)\left(1+m_c\right)=\left(1+m_b\right)\left(2+m_a+m_c\right)
\end{gathered}\)$

13790.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
13790.text: A ball moving with velocity $2 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$ collides head on with another stationary ball of double the mass. If coefficient of restitution is 0.5 , then their velocities (in $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ ) after collision will be :
13790.sol:
Let mass of first ball be $m$ i.e. $m_1=m$
Mass of second ball $\mathrm{m}_2=2 \mathrm{ m}$
Velocity of first ball before collision $\mathrm{u}_1=2 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$
Velocity of second ball before collision $\mathrm{u}_2=\mathrm{om} / \mathrm{s}$
Given : $\mathrm{e}=0.5$
So, velocity of first ball after collision $\mathrm{v}_1=\frac{\left(\mathrm{m}_1-\mathrm{em}_2\right) \mathrm{u}_1+(1+\mathrm{e}) \mathrm{m}_2 \mathrm{u}_2}{\mathrm{ m}_1+\mathrm{m}_2}\therefore \mathrm{v}_1=\frac{[\mathrm{m}-0.5(2 \mathrm{ m})](2)+(1+0.5)(2 \mathrm{ m})(0)}{\mathrm{m}+2 \mathrm{ m}}=\mathrm{om} / \mathrm{s}$
Velocity of second ball after collision $\mathrm{v}_2=\frac{\left(\mathrm{m}_2-\mathrm{em}_1\right) \mathrm{u}_2+(1+\mathrm{e}) \mathrm{m}_1 \mathrm{u}_1}{\mathrm{ m}_1+\mathrm{m}_2}\therefore \mathrm{v}_2=\frac{[2 \mathrm{ m}-0.5 \mathrm{ m}](0)+(1+0.5)(\mathrm{m})(2)}{\mathrm{m}+2 \mathrm{ m}}=1 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$
Correct answer is option A.

13847.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
13847.text:
A ball falls freely from a height of $180 \mathrm{ m}$ on to a hard horizontal floor and repeatedly bounces. If the coefficient of restitution is 0.5 , the average speed and average velocity of the ball before it ceases to rebound are respectively
(acceleration due to gravity $=10 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$ )
13847.sol: When ball dropped from height $h$, then time taken to reach the ground $$ t_0=\sqrt{\frac{2 h}{g}} \text{ and speed, } v_0=\sqrt{2 g h} $$ After first collision, its speed will become $v_1=e v_0=e \sqrt{2 g h}$ where, $e=$ coefficient of restitution. Now, the ball will go up and will take time $t_1$, when it stops $$ \begin{aligned} & v=u+a t \\ & \quad 0=v_1-g t_1 \\ & t_1=\frac{v_1}{g} \end{aligned} $$ It will come down and take same time $t_1$ before second collision. So, time taken between first and second collision is $2 t_1$. Similarly, time taken between second and third collision will be $2 t_3=\frac{2 v_2}{g}$ Total time before it ceaser to rebound $$ \begin{aligned} & T=t_0+2 t_1+2 t_2+\ldots \ldots \ldots \\ & T=t_0+\frac{2 v_1}{g}+\frac{2 v_2}{g}+\ldots \ldots \ldots \\ & T=t_0+\frac{2 e v_0}{g}+\frac{2 e^2 v_0}{g}+\ldots \ldots \ldots \\ & \quad\left\{\text{ as } v_2=e v_1=e^2 v_0\right\} \\ & T=\sqrt{\frac{2 h}{g}}\left[1+2 e\left(1+e+e^2+e^3+\ldots\right)\right] \\ & \left\{\text{ as } v_0=\sqrt{\frac{2 h}{g}}\right\} \end{aligned} $$ It forms a GP, $$ \begin{aligned} T & =\sqrt{\frac{2 h}{g}}\left[1+2 e\left(\frac{1}{1-e}\right)\right] \\ T & =\sqrt{\frac{2 h}{g}}\left(\frac{1+e}{1-e}\right) \end{aligned} $$ Given, $h=180 \mathrm{~m}$ and $e=0.5$ $$ \begin{aligned} T & =\sqrt{\frac{2 \times 180}{10}}\left(\frac{1+0.5}{1-0.5}\right) \end{aligned} $$ $$ T=6 \times 3=18 \mathrm{~s} $$ Calculation of distance in entire motion initial height $h_0=h$ After first collision $=h_1$ As $$ \begin{aligned} & e=\frac{v}{u}=\sqrt{\frac{2 g h_1}{2 g h_0}}=\sqrt{\frac{h_1}{h}} \\ & \quad h_1=e^2 h, \text{ similarly } h_2=e^2\left(e^2 h\right) \\ & h_2=e^4 h \end{aligned} $$ Total distance, $$ \begin{aligned} & H=h_0+2 h_1+2 h_2+\ldots \ldots \\ & H=h+2 e^2 h+2 e^4 h+\ldots \ldots \\ & H=h\left[1+2 e^2\left(1+e^2+e^4+\ldots \ldots\right)\right] \\ & H=h\left[1+2 e^2\left(\frac{1}{1-e^2}\right)\right] \\ & H=h\left(\frac{1+e^2}{1-e^2}\right) \\ & H=180\left(\frac{1+\frac{1}{4}}{1-\frac{1}{4}}\right), e=0.5=\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned} $$ $\begin{aligned} & H=180 \times \frac{5}{3} \\ & H=300 \mathrm{~m} \\ & \text{ Average speed, } v=\frac{\text{ Total distance }}{\text{ Time }} \\ & v=\frac{300}{18}=\frac{50}{3} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \\ & \text{ Average velocity, } v=\frac{\text{ Total displacement }}{\text{ Time }} \\ & v=\frac{180}{18}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \\ & \end{aligned}$

19540.subject: Chemistry
19540.text: Identify products [P$_1$] and [P$_2$] formed when Benzonitrile undergoes the following reactions.
19540.sol:
1. Formation of [X]: Benzonitrile ($C_6H_5CN$) undergoes Stephen reduction when treated with $SnCl_2/HCl$ in ether, forming an imine intermediate. Subsequent acid hydrolysis ($H_3O^+$) yields benzaldehyde ($C_6H_5CHO$). Thus, [X] is benzaldehyde.

2. Formation of [P$_1$]: Benzaldehyde reacts with $HCN$ to undergo nucleophilic addition, forming benzaldehyde cyanohydrin ($C_6H_5CH(OH)CN$). Acid hydrolysis ($H_3O^+$) of the nitrile group converts it into a carboxylic acid group, yielding $\alpha$-hydroxy phenylacetic acid ($C_6H_5CH(OH)COOH$). Thus, [P$_1$] is $\alpha$-hydroxy phenylacetic acid.

3. Formation of [P$_2$]: Benzaldehyde does not have any $\alpha$-hydrogen atoms. When treated with a concentrated base ($50\%\ NaOH$), it undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction (a disproportionation reaction). Two moles of benzaldehyde react to form one mole of benzyl alcohol ($C_6H_5CH_2OH$) and one mole of sodium benzoate ($C_6H_5COO^-Na^+$), which is the salt. Thus, [P$_2$] is benzyl alcohol.

Answer: [P$_1$] $\alpha$–Hydroxy phenylacetic acid and [P$_2$] Benzyl alcohol

19686.subject: Chemistry
19686.text: Which of the following hexoses will form the same osazone when treated with excess phenyl hydrazine?
19686.sol:
Osazone formation involves the reaction of the first two carbon atoms of a sugar with phenylhydrazine. Sugars that differ only in the configuration at the first and second carbon atoms (epimers at C-2) form the same osazone.

D-glucose, D-fructose, and D-mannose share the same configuration at carbons C-3, C-4, C-5, and C-6. Specifically, D-glucose and D-mannose are C-2 epimers, and D-fructose is a ketose that, upon reaction with phenylhydrazine, undergoes tautomerization to form the same intermediate as D-glucose and D-mannose.

Since D-glucose, D-fructose, and D-mannose have identical configurations at C-3, C-4, C-5, and C-6, they yield the same osazone product.

Answer: D-glucose, D-fructose and D-mannose

21908.subject: Mathematics
21908.text: A determinant of the second order is made with elements 0 and 1. What is the probability that the determinant made is non-negative?
21908.sol:
A second order determinant is given by $\begin{vmatrix} a \text{ and } b \\ c \text{ and } d \end{vmatrix} = ad - bc$.

Each element $a, b, c, d$ can take values from the set $\{0, 1\}$. Since there are 4 positions and each position has 2 choices, the total number of possible determinants is $2^4 = 16$.

We want to find the number of cases where $ad - bc \ge 0$, which is equivalent to $ad \ge bc$.

Let us list the possible values of $ad$ and $bc$:
If $ad = 1$, then $a=1$ and $d=1$ (1 case).
If $ad = 0$, then $(a,d) \in \{(0,0), (0,1), (1,0)\}$ (3 cases).
Similarly, $bc = 1$ occurs in 1 case and $bc = 0$ occurs in 3 cases.

We evaluate $ad \ge bc$ for all combinations:
1. If $ad = 1$ (1 case), then $bc$ can be 0 or 1. If $bc=0$ (3 cases), $1 \ge 0$ is true. If $bc=1$ (1 case), $1 \ge 1$ is true. So $1 \times (3 + 1) = 4$ cases.
2. If $ad = 0$ (3 cases), then $bc$ must be 0 for $ad \ge bc$ to hold. Since $bc=0$ occurs in 3 cases, we have $3 \times 3 = 9$ cases.

Total favorable cases = $4 + 9 = 13$.

The probability is $\dfrac{13}{16}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{13}{16}$

22965.subject: Physics
22965.text: What is the maximum speed with which a vehicle can take the turn on a curved frictionless smooth road of width 4 m , without skidding, if the radius of the circular curve of the road is 9 m and the outer edge of the road above the inner edge is 40 cm high? [given $g=\mathrm{1 0} \mathrm{ms}^{-2}$ ]
22965.sol:
For a vehicle moving on a banked road without skidding, the required centripetal force is provided by the horizontal component of the normal reaction. The angle of banking $\theta$ is given by $\tan \theta = \dfrac{h}{b}$, where $h$ is the height of the outer edge above the inner edge and $b$ is the width of the road.

Given $h = 40 \text{ cm} = 0.4 \text{ m}$ and $b = 4 \text{ m}$, we have $\tan \theta = \dfrac{0.4}{4} = 0.1$.

The maximum speed $v$ for a banked road without friction is given by $v = \sqrt{rg \tan \theta}$, where $r$ is the radius of the curve and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

Substituting the given values $r = 9 \text{ m}$, $g = 10 \text{ ms}^{-2}$, and $\tan \theta = 0.1$:

$v = \sqrt{9 \times 10 \times 0.1} = \sqrt{9} = 3 \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

Answer: $\mathrm{3} \mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$

23070.text: Three long straight wires $A, B$ and $C$ are carrying currents as shown in figure, then the resultant force on $B$ is directed
options: perpendicular to the plane of paper and outward
perpendicular to the plane of paper and inward
23070.sol:
The magnetic force between two current carrying wires for current in same direction is attractive.
Thus, force on $B$ due to the magnetic field produced due to wire A$ is \begin{aligned} F_{\mathrm{A}} &=B_{A} I_{B} l=\frac{\mu_{0} \times I_{A}}{2 \pi d} \times I_{B} \times l \\
&=\frac{\mu_{0} \times 1 \times 2 \times l}{2 \pi d}=\frac{2 \mu_{0} l}{2 \pi d}, \text{ towards } A \quad \ldots(\text{ i })
\end{aligned}$ Similarly, force due to field of wire $C$, $\begin{aligned}& F_{C}=B_{C} I_{B} l=\frac{\mu_{0} I_{C} I_{B} l}{2 \pi d}=\frac{\mu_{0} \times 3 \times 2 \times l}{2 \pi d}\\
\Rightarrow \quad & F_{C}=\frac{6 \mu_{0} l}{2 \pi d}, \text{ towards } C
\end{aligned}$ From Eqs. (i) and (ii) we get F_{C}>F_{A}\therefore$ The resultant force on $B$ is directed towards $C$.$

23314.subject: Physics
23314.text: From the equations given below select the correct equation representing the displacement of a particle undergoing a periodic motion. [$y$ - displacement; a - amplitude $T$ - Period; $\omega$ - angular velocity; $t$-time]
23314.sol:
The general equation for the displacement of a particle undergoing simple harmonic motion is given by $y = a \sin(\omega t + \phi)$, where $\omega$ is the angular frequency and $t$ is the time.

The relationship between angular frequency $\omega$ and the time period $T$ is defined as $\omega = \dfrac{2 \pi}{T}$.

Substituting this expression for $\omega$ into the general displacement equation, we get $y = a \sin\left(\dfrac{2 \pi}{T} t\right)$.

Rearranging the terms inside the sine function, we obtain $y = a \sin\left(\dfrac{2 \pi t}{T}\right)$.

Answer: $y=a \sin \left[\dfrac{(2 \pi \mathrm{t})}{T}\right]$

28678.subject: Chemistry
28678.text: Consider the transition metal ions $\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}, \mathrm{Cr}^{3+}, \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ and $\mathrm{Co}^{3+}$ and all form low spin octahedral complexes. The correct decreasing order of unpaired electrons in their respective d-orbitals of the complexes is
28678.sol:
For low spin octahedral complexes, electrons fill the $t_{2g}$ orbitals first before pairing or moving to $e_g$ orbitals. The configuration depends on the number of d-electrons.
For $Cr^{3+}$: Electronic configuration is $3d^3$. In an octahedral field, the configuration is $t_{2g}^3 e_g^0$. Number of unpaired electrons ($n$) = 3.
For $Mn^{3+}$: Electronic configuration is $3d^4$. For low spin, the configuration is $t_{2g}^4 e_g^0$. Number of unpaired electrons ($n$) = 2.
For $Fe^{3+}$: Electronic configuration is $3d^5$. For low spin, the configuration is $t_{2g}^5 e_g^0$. Number of unpaired electrons ($n$) = 1.
For $Co^{3+}$: Electronic configuration is $3d^6$. For low spin, the configuration is $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$. Number of unpaired electrons ($n$) = 0.
Comparing the number of unpaired electrons:
$Cr^{3+} (3) > Mn^{3+} (2) > Fe^{3+} (1) > Co^{3+} (0)$.
The correct decreasing order is $Cr^{3+} > Mn^{3+} > Fe^{3+} > Co^{3+}$.

32873.text: A wire of length $22m$ is to be cut into two pieces. One of the pieces is to be made into a square and the other into an equilateral triangle. Then, the length of the side of the equilateral triangle, so that the combined area of the square and the equilateral triangle is minimum, is
32873.sol:
Let the side of square be $\dfrac{22 - l}{4}$ and side of triangle be $\dfrac{l}{3}$ ,

So, total area is given by $\Delta = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}{\left(\dfrac{l}{3}\right)}^{2} + {\left(\dfrac{22 - l}{4}\right)}^{2}$

$⇒ \Delta = \dfrac{1}{12\sqrt{3}} \cdot {l}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{16}{\left(22 - l\right)}^{2}$

Differentiating with respect to $l$ to get maxima and minima points,

$⇒ \dfrac{d\Delta}{dl} = \dfrac{1}{6\sqrt{3}} \cdot l - \dfrac{1}{8}\left(22 - l\right) = 0$ $⇒ l = \dfrac{66\sqrt{3}}{4 + 3\sqrt{3}}$

Also$\dfrac{{d}^{2}\Delta}{d{l}^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{6\sqrt{3}} + \dfrac{1}{8}$ ($+ ve$. which is case of minima)

So, side of triangle will be $= \dfrac{l}{3} = \dfrac{22\sqrt{3}}{4 + 3\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{66}{4\sqrt{3} + 9}$

33006.text: If the tangent at a point $P$, with parameter $t$, on the curve $x = 4{t}^{2} + 3, y = 8{t}^{3} - 1, t \in R,$ meets the curve again at a point $Q$, then the coordinates of $Q$ are :

Given $P\left(4{t}^{2} + 3, 8{t}^{3} - 1\right)$

$\dfrac{\dfrac{dy}{dt}}{\dfrac{dx}{dt}} = \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3t$ (slope of tangent at $P$)

Let $Q = \left(4{\lambda}^{2} + 3, 8{\lambda}^{3} - 1\right)$

Slope of $PQ = 3t$

$\dfrac{8{t}^{3} - 8{\lambda}^{3}}{4{t}^{2} - 4{\lambda}^{2}} = 3t$

$⇒$ ${t}^{2} + t\lambda - 2{\lambda}^{2} = 0$

$\left(t - \lambda\right)\left(t + 2\lambda\right) = 0$

$t = \lambda$ or $\lambda = \dfrac{- t}{2}$

$∴$ $Q\left[{t}^{2} + 3, - {t}^{3} - 1\right]$

33775.text: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of the equation $2 z^2-3 z-2 \mathrm{i}=0$, where $\mathrm{i}=\sqrt{-1}$, then $16 \cdot \operatorname{Re}\left(\frac{\alpha^{19}+\beta^{19}+\alpha^{11}+\beta^{11}}{\alpha^{15}+\beta^{15}}\right) \cdot \operatorname{lm}\left(\frac{\alpha^{19}+\beta^{19}+\alpha^{11}+\beta^{11}}{\alpha^{15}+\beta^{15}}\right)$ is equal to
33775.sol:
$2 z^2-3 z-2 i=0$ ...(i)
$2\left(z-\frac{i}{z}\right)=3$
As $\alpha, \beta$ are roots of (i)
$\begin{aligned}
& \alpha-\frac{i}{\alpha}=\frac{3}{2} \\
& \Rightarrow \alpha^2-\frac{1}{\alpha^2}-2 i=\frac{9}{4} \\
& \Rightarrow \alpha^2-\frac{1}{\alpha^2}=\frac{9}{4}+2 i
\end{aligned}$

Squaring both sides
$\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \alpha^4+\frac{1}{\alpha^4}-2=\frac{81}{16}-4+9 i \\
& \Rightarrow \alpha^4+\frac{1}{\alpha^4}=\frac{49}{16}+9 i
\end{aligned}$

Similarly, $\beta^4+\frac{1}{\beta^4}=\frac{49}{16}+9 i \begin{aligned}
& \frac{\alpha^{19}+\beta^{19}+\alpha^{11}+\beta^{11}}{\alpha^{15}+\beta^{15}} \\
& =\frac{\alpha^{15}\left(\alpha^4+\frac{1}{\alpha^4}\right)+\beta^{15}\left(\beta^4+\frac{1}{\beta^4}\right)}{\alpha^{15}+\beta^{15}} \\
& =\frac{49}{16}+9 i \\
& \operatorname{Re}\left(\frac{\alpha^{19}+\beta^{19}+\alpha^{11}+\beta^{11}}{\alpha^{15}+\beta^{15}}\right)=\frac{49}{16} \\
& \operatorname{Im}\left(\frac{\alpha^{19}+\beta^{19}+\alpha^{11}+\beta^{11}}{\alpha^{15}+\beta^{15}}\right)=9 \\
& \Rightarrow 16 \operatorname{Re}\left(\frac{\alpha^{19}+\beta^{19}+\alpha^{11}+\beta^{11}}{\alpha^{15}+\beta^{15}}\right) \cdot \operatorname{lm}\left(\frac{\alpha^{19}+\beta^{19}+\alpha^{11}+\beta^{11}}{\alpha^{15}+\beta^{15}}\right) \\
& =16 \times \frac{49}{16} \times 9 \\
& =441
\end{aligned}$

options: System has infinite number of solution if $\lambda = 1$ and $\mu = 13$
System has unique solution if $\lambda \ne 1$ and $\mu \ne 13$
34472.sol:
Given: 

$x + y + z = 5$

$x + 2y + {\lambda}^{2}z = 9$

$x + 3y + \lambdaz = \mu$

$⇒ △ = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & {\lambda}^{2} \\ 1 & 3 & \lambda\end{cases}\right|$

$⇒ △ = 2\lambda - 3{\lambda}^{2} - \lambda + {\lambda}^{2} + 1$

$⇒ △ = - 2{\lambda}^{2} + \lambda + 1$

We know that for infinite solutions, $△ = 0 \text{ and } {△}_{1} = {△}_{2} = {△}_{3} = 0$

$⇒ - 2{\lambda}^{2} + \lambda + 1 = 0$

$⇒ 2{\lambda}^{2} - \lambda - 1 = 0$

$⇒ \left(\lambda - 1\right)\left(2\lambda + 1\right) = 0$

$⇒ \lambda = 1, \dfrac{- 1}{2}$

Now, finding ${△}_{1}$ for $\lambda = 1$ we get,

${\Delta}_{1} = \left|\begin{cases}5 & 1 & 1 \\ 9 & 2 & 1 \\ \mu & 3 & 1\end{cases}\right|$

$⇒ {\Delta}_{1} = \mu - 13$

And for $\lambda = \dfrac{- 1}{2}$ we get,

${\Delta}_{1} = \left|\begin{cases}5 & 1 & 1 \\ 9 & 2 & \dfrac{1}{4} \\ \mu & 3 & \dfrac{- 1}{2}\end{cases}\right| = \dfrac{1}{4}\left|\begin{cases}5 & 1 & 4 \\ 9 & 2 & 1 \\ \mu & 3 & - 2\end{cases}\right| = \dfrac{7}{4}\left(13 - \mu\right)$

So, for $\lambda \ne 1 \text{ and } \mu \ne 13$ system has no solution,

Hence, option $\left(C\right)$ is the correct answer.

34788.text: Let $y = y ( x )$ be the solution of the differential equation $\left(\left(x + 2\right){e}^{\left(\dfrac{y + 1}{x + 2}\right)} + \left(y + 1\right)\right)dx = \left(x + 2\right)dy, y\left(1\right) = 1 .$ If the domain of $y = y\left(x\right)$ is an open interval $( \alpha, \beta ) ,$ then $| \alpha + \beta |$ is equal to ___________.
34788.sol:
The given differential equation is $\left(\left(x + 2\right){e}^{\left(\dfrac{y + 1}{x + 2}\right)} + \left(y + 1\right)\right)dx = \left(x + 2\right)dy, y\left(1\right) = 1$

Let, $y + 1 = Y ⇒ dy = dY$ and $x + 2 = X ⇒ dx = dX$ and at $y = 1, Y = 2$ and at $x = 1, X = 3 .$

Thus, the differential equation becomes $\left(Xe\dfrac{Y}{X} + Y\right)dX = XdY$

$⇒ XdY - YdX = Xe\dfrac{Y}{X}dX$

$⇒ \dfrac{\left(XdY - YdX\right)}{{X}^{2}} = \left(\dfrac{X{e}^{\dfrac{Y}{X}}}{{X}^{2}}\right)dX$

$⇒ \dfrac{d}{dX}\left(\dfrac{Y}{X}\right) = \left(\dfrac{X{e}^{\dfrac{Y}{X}}}{{X}^{2}}\right)dX$

$⇒ d\left(\dfrac{Y}{X}\right){e}^{- \dfrac{Y}{X}} = \dfrac{dX}{X}$

Integrating both sides w.r.to $X,$ we get $∫ d\left(\dfrac{Y}{X}\right){e}^{- \dfrac{Y}{X}} = ∫ \dfrac{dX}{X}$

$⇒ - {e}^{- \dfrac{Y}{X}} = {\log}_{e}\left|X\right| + c$

Given, at $X = 3, Y = 2$

$⇒ - {e}^{- \dfrac{2}{3}} = {\log}_{e}\left|3\right| + c$

$⇒ c = - {e}^{- \dfrac{2}{3}} - {\log}_{e}\left|3\right|$

$⇒ - {e}^{- \dfrac{Y}{X}} = {\log}_{e}\left|X\right| - {e}^{- \dfrac{2}{3}} - {\log}_{e}3$

${e}^{- \dfrac{Y}{X}} = e\dfrac{2}{3} + {\log}_{e}3 - {\log}_{e}\left|X\right| > 0$

${\log}_{e}\left|X\right| < e\dfrac{2}{3} + {\log}_{e}3$

Let, $\lambda = \left(e\dfrac{2}{3} + {\log}_{e}3\right)$ then, we have $\left|x + 2\right| < {e}^{\lambda}$

$⇒ - {e}^{\lambda} < x + 2 < {e}^{\lambda}$

$⇒ - {e}^{\lambda} - 2 < x < {e}^{\lambda} - 2$

Thus, the domain of the function is $\left(- {e}^{\lambda} - 2, {e}^{\lambda} - 2\right) .$

Given, the domain of the function is $\left(\alpha, \beta\right),$ hence $\alpha = - {e}^{\lambda} - 2 \text{ and } \beta = {e}^{\lambda} - 2$

$⇒ \alpha + \beta = - {e}^{\lambda} - 2 + {e}^{\lambda} - 2 = - 4$

$⇒ | \alpha + \beta | = 4 .$

37017.subject: Mathematics
37017.text: If the sum of the first $10$ terms of the series $\dfrac{1}{1 + 1^4 \times 4} + \dfrac{2}{1 + 2^4 \times 4} + \dfrac{3}{1 + 3^4 \times 4} + \dfrac{4}{1 + 4^4 \times 4} + \ldots$ is $\dfrac{m}{n}$, $\gcd(m, n) = 1$, then $m + n$ is equal to :
37017.sol:
The general term of the series is $T_r = \dfrac{r}{1 + 4r^4}$.

Factorizing the denominator:

$1 + 4r^4 = (1 + 2r^2)^2 - 4r^2 = (2r^2 - 2r + 1)(2r^2 + 2r + 1)$

Thus, $T_r = \dfrac{r}{(2r^2 - 2r + 1)(2r^2 + 2r + 1)}$

Multiplying and dividing by $4$:

$T_r = \dfrac{1}{4} \left[ \dfrac{4r}{(2r^2 - 2r + 1)(2r^2 + 2r + 1)} \right]$

$T_r = \dfrac{1}{4} \left[ \dfrac{1}{2r^2 - 2r + 1} - \dfrac{1}{2r^2 + 2r + 1} \right]$

The sum of the first $10$ terms is:

$S_{10} = \sum_{r=1}^{10} T_r = \dfrac{1}{4} \sum_{r=1}^{10} \left( \dfrac{1}{2r^2 - 2r + 1} - \dfrac{1}{2(r+1)^2 - 2(r+1) + 1} \right)$

This is a telescoping series, so all intermediate terms cancel out:

$S_{10} = \dfrac{1}{4} \left[ \left( \dfrac{1}{1} - \dfrac{1}{5} \right) + \left( \dfrac{1}{5} - \dfrac{1}{13} \right) + \ldots + \left( \dfrac{1}{2(10)^2 - 2(10) + 1} - \dfrac{1}{2(10)^2 + 2(10) + 1} \right) \right]$

$S_{10} = \dfrac{1}{4} \left[ 1 - \dfrac{1}{221} \right] = \dfrac{1}{4} \left( \dfrac{220}{221} \right) = \dfrac{55}{221}$

Given $S_{10} = \dfrac{m}{n}$ and $\gcd(m, n) = 1$.

Here, $m = 55$ and $n = 221$. Since $55 = 5 \times 11$ and $221 = 13 \times 17$, $\gcd(55, 221) = 1$.

Therefore, $m + n = 55 + 221 = 276$.

Answer: $276$

37507.subject: Mathematics
37507.text: If the mean deviation about the median of the numbers $\mathrm{k}, 2 \mathrm{k}, 3 \mathrm{k}, \ldots. ., 1000 \mathrm{k}$ is 500, then $\mathrm{k}^{2}$ is equal to :
37507.sol:
The sequence $k, 2k, 3k, \ldots, 1000k$ has 1000 terms.
The median is $\frac{500k + 501k}{2} = \frac{1001k}{2}$.
The mean deviation is $MD = \frac{1}{1000}\sum_{i=1}^{1000}|ik - \text{median}|$.
For $i \leq 500$: deviation = $\frac{1001k}{2} - ik$, giving $\sum_{i=1}^{500}(\frac{1001}{2} - i) = 125000$.
By symmetry, the sum for $i \geq 501$ is also $125000$.
Thus $MD = \frac{k}{1000} \cdot 250000 = 250k = 500$, so $k = 2$ and $k^2 = 4$.

38987.text: If $917Å$  be the lowest wavelength of Lyman series then the lowest wavelength of Balmer series will be $Å$.
38987.sol:
Using Rydberg's formula,

$\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R{Z}^{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{{n}^{2}1} - \dfrac{1}{{n}^{2}2}\right)$

For the lowest wavelength in Lyman series, ${n}_{1} = 1, {n}_{2} = \infty$.

$\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R{Z}^{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{{1}^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{{\infty}^{2}}\right) = R{Z}^{2}$

For Balmer series, ${n}_{1} = 2, {n}_{2} = \infty$

$\dfrac{1}{\lambda '} = R{Z}^{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{{2}^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{{\infty}^{2}}\right) = \dfrac{R{Z}^{2}}{4}$

So,

$\dfrac{1}{\lambda '} = \dfrac{1}{4\lambda} ⇒ \lambda ' = 4 \times 917\overset{}{Å = 3668Å}$

39628.text: As shown in the figure the voltmeter reads $2V$ across $5Ω$ resistor. The resistance of the voltmeter is _____ $Ω$
39628.sol:
Let the resistance of the voltmeter be $RΩ$. The voltmeter is in parallel with the $5Ω$. So the total resistance in the circuit is

$\left(\dfrac{5R}{5 + R} + 2\right)Ω$

Applying Ohm's law in the whole circuit, $V = IR$,

$I = \left(\dfrac{3}{2 + \dfrac{5R}{5 + R}}\right)A$

It is given that the potential difference across $5Ω$ is $2V$.

Thus, by Ohm's law,

$\left(\dfrac{3}{2 + \dfrac{5R}{5 + R}}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{5R}{R + 5}\right) = 2 ⇒ \dfrac{15 + 3R}{10 + 7R} \times \dfrac{5R}{5 + R} = 2 ⇒ 15R = 20 + 14R ⇒ R = 20Ω$

41411.subject: Physics
41411.text:
A long cylindrical conductor with large cross section carries an electric current distributed uniformly over its cross-section. Magnetic field due to this current is :
A. maximum at either ends of the conductor and minimum at the midpoint
B. maximum at the axis of the conductor
C. minimum at the surface of the conductor
D. minimum at the axis of the conductor
E. same at all points in the cross-section of the conductor
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
41411.sol:
For a long cylindrical conductor with uniform current distribution, apply Ampere's law to find the magnetic field.
At distance $r$ from the axis (inside the conductor, $r < R$): $B(r) = \frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi R^2}$ (proportional to $r$)
At the axis ($r = 0$): $B = 0$ (minimum)
At the surface ($r = R$): $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi R}$ (maximum)
Analyzing the statements:
A. Maximum at ends and minimum at midpoint - FALSE. This describes behavior along the axis, but the magnetic field depends on radial distance, not axial position.
B. Maximum at the axis of the conductor - FALSE. The field is zero at the axis.
C. Minimum at the surface of the conductor - FALSE. The field is maximum at the surface.
D. Minimum at the axis of the conductor - TRUE. The field is zero at $r = 0$, making it the minimum.
E. Same at all points in the cross-section - FALSE. The field varies from 0 at the axis to maximum at the surface.
Only D is correct.

41725.text: A magnetic compass needle oscillates $30$ times per minute at a place where the dip is $45 °$ and $40$ times per minute where the dip is $30 °$. ${f}_{2} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\dfrac{M{B}_{2}cos30 °}{I}}$

$\dfrac{{f}_{1}}{{f}_{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{{B}_{1}cos45 °}{{B}_{2}cos30 °}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{30}^{2}}{{40}^{2}} = \dfrac{{B}_{1}cos45 °}{{B}_{2}cos30 °}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{B}_{1}}{{B}_{2}} = \dfrac{900 \times cos30 °}{1600 \times cos45 °}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{B}_{1}}{{B}_{2}} = 0.688 \approx 0.7$

41896.subject: Physics
41896.text: Surface tension of two liquids (having same densities), $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$, are measured using capillary rise method utilizing two tubes with inner radii of $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ where $r_{1}>r_{2}$. The measured liquid heights in these tubes are $h_{1}$ and $h_{2}$ respectively. [Ignore the weight of the liquid about the lowest point of miniscus]. The heights $h_{1}$ and $h_{2}$ and surfaces tensions $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ satisfy the relation:
41896.sol:
For capillary rise, the height of liquid in a tube is given by: $h = \frac{2T\cos\theta}{\rho g r}$, where $T$ is surface tension and $r$ is the tube radius.

For two liquids with equal density and contact angles:
$h_1 = \frac{2T_1\cos\theta}{\rho g r_1}$ and $h_2 = \frac{2T_2\cos\theta}{\rho g r_2}$

Taking the ratio: $\frac{h_1}{h_2} = \frac{T_1}{T_2} \times \frac{r_2}{r_1}$

Since $r_1 > r_2$, we have $\frac{r_2}{r_1} < 1$. The capillary rise is inversely proportional to tube radius, so the smaller radius tube will have greater height. Since the liquids are measured to have heights $h_1$ and $h_2$ with $r_1 > r_2$, and they have the same density, the empirical relation shows that both liquids rise to different heights inversely proportional to their radii. For liquids with the same density measured in different tubes, if the heights and radii satisfy the capillary rise equation, the surface tensions must be equal: $T_1 = T_2$, and $h_1 < h_2$ since $r_1 > r_2$.

43234.subject: Physics
43234.text: A solid cylinder is released from rest from the top of an inclined plane of inclination $30 °$ and length $60cm$. If the cylinder rolls without slipping, its speed upon reaching the bottom of the inclined plane is ______ $m{s}^{- 1}$. (Given $g = 10m{s}^{- 2}$)
43234.sol:
Let speed of cylinder upon reaching the bottom of the inclined plane be $v$.

Here, gain in kinetic energy$=$loss in potential energy

So, $\dfrac{1}{2}I{\omega}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} = mglsin\theta$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{m{r}^{2}}{2}\right){\omega}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} = mglsin30 °$

For pure rolling, $v = r\omega$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{m{r}^{2}}{2}\right){\left(\dfrac{v}{r}\right)}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} = mglsin30 °$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{4}m{v}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} = mglsin30 ° ⇒ \dfrac{3}{4}m{v}^{2} = \dfrac{mgl}{2} ⇒ v = \sqrt{\dfrac{4gl}{6}}$

Putting the values, we have

$⇒ v = \sqrt{\dfrac{4 \times 10 \times 0 . 6}{6}} = 2m{s}^{- 1}$

44387.text: Two harmonic waves moving in the same direction superimpose to form a wave $\mathrm{x}=\mathrm{a} \cos (1.5 \mathrm{t}) \cos (50.5 \mathrm{t})$ where $t$ is in seconds. Find the period with which they beat (close to nearest integer)
44387.sol:
The given equation can be written as
$\mathrm{x}=\frac{\mathrm{a}}{2} \cos [1.5+50.5] \mathrm{t}+\frac{\mathrm{a}}{2} \cos [50.5-1.5]$
$x=\frac{a}{2} \cos [52 t]+\frac{a}{2} \cos [49 t]$
Here, $2 \pi \mathrm{f}_1 \& 2 \pi \mathrm{f}_2=49$
$\mathrm{f}_1=\frac{52}{2 \pi}, \mathrm{f}_2=\frac{49}{2 \pi}$
$\therefore \mathrm{f}_{\text{Bat }}=\mathrm{f}_1-\mathrm{f}_2=\frac{3}{2 \pi} \mathrm{~Hz}$
$\therefore \mathrm{T}_{\text{Beat }}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}_{\text{Beat }}}=\frac{2 \pi}{3} \mathrm{sec}$
$=2.09 \mathrm{sec} \approx 2 \mathrm{sec}$

Viscous force acting on spherical drop
$F_v=6 \pi \eta r v \therefore$ Terminal velocity, $v=\frac{2}{9} \frac{r^2(\sigma-\rho) g}{\eta}$
where, $\eta=$ coefficient of viscosity of liquid
$\sigma=$ density of material of spherical drop
$\rho=$ density of liquid
Power imparted by viscous force
= Rate of production of heat
$\begin{aligned} P & =\frac{d H}{d t}=F_v \cdot v=6 \pi \eta r v^2 \\ & =6 \pi \eta r \cdot\left(\frac{2}{9} \frac{r^2(\sigma-\rho) g}{\eta}\right)^2 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{d H}{d t} & \propto r^5\end{aligned}$

54835.subject: Chemistry
54835.text:
Identify product 'B' in following series of reactions
2-methylpropan-2-ol $\xrightarrow[\large{363\ \text{K}}]{\large{20\%\ \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4}}$ A $\xrightarrow[\large{\text{Conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4}]{\large{\text{H}_2\text{O}\ \ \Delta}}$ B
54835.sol:
The starting material, 2-methylpropan-2-ol, is a tertiary alcohol. On heating with $20\%H_2SO_4$ at $363\ \text{K}$, it undergoes acid-catalyzed dehydration to form an alkene, 2-methylpropene (product A).

$(CH_3)_3C-OH \xrightarrow{H^+, \Delta} (CH_3)_2C=CH_2 + H_2O$

Product A is 2-methylpropene.

When 2-methylpropene is treated with water in the presence of concentrated $H_2SO_4$ and heat, it undergoes acid-catalyzed hydration. The addition of water follows Markovnikov's rule, proceeding via the formation of a stable tertiary carbocation.

$(CH_3)_2C=CH_2 + H^+ \rightarrow (CH_3)_3C^+$

$(CH_3)_3C^+ + H_2O \rightarrow (CH_3)_3C-OH + H^+$

The final product B is 2-methylpropan-2-ol, which is commonly known as tert-butyl alcohol.

Answer: tert-Butylalcohol

55450.text: Which component of DNA carries genetic information?
55450.sol:
The genetic information in DNA is stored in the specific sequence of its nitrogenous bases (adenine, thymine, cytosine, and guanine).

The sugar and phosphate groups form the structural backbone of the DNA molecule, while hydrogen bonds hold the two complementary strands together.

Therefore, the sequence of nitrogenous bases is responsible for carrying genetic information.

Answer: Sequence of nitrogenous bases

56639.subject: Chemistry
56639.text: Which of the following factors may be regarded as the main cause of lanthanide contraction?
options: Poor shielding of one of 4f electron by another in the sub-shell.
Effective shielding of one of 4f electrons by another in the subshell
Poorer shielding of 5d electrons by 4f electrons
Greater shielding of 5d electrons by 4f electrons
56639.sol:
Lanthanide contraction refers to the steady decrease in the atomic and ionic radii of lanthanides with an increase in atomic number.

As we move along the lanthanide series, the nuclear charge increases by one unit at each step, and the new electron enters the 4f subshell. The shape of the 4f orbitals is highly diffused, which results in a very poor shielding effect. Consequently, the shielding of one 4f electron by another in the same subshell is inadequate to counterbalance the increased nuclear charge.

Due to this poor shielding, the effective nuclear charge experienced by the outermost electrons increases, pulling them closer to the nucleus and causing a contraction in size.

Answer: Poor shielding of one of 4f electron by another in the sub-shell.

56862.subject: Chemistry
56862.text:
A hypothetical galvanic cell is
$\ominus_{\mathrm{A}_{(\mathrm{s})}}\left|\mathrm{A}^{+}(1 \mathrm{M})\right|\left|\mathrm{B}^{+2}(1 \mathrm{M})\right| \mathrm{B}_{(\mathrm{s})}^{\oplus}$
and emf of cell is positive. What is the possible cell reaction?
56862.sol:
Cell notation: $\ominus_{\mathrm{A}_{(\mathrm{s})}}|\mathrm{A}^{+}(1\ \mathrm{M})||\mathrm{B}^{+2}(1\ \mathrm{M})|\mathrm{B}_{(\mathrm{s})}^{\oplus}$

The anode (left side) shows oxidation of $\mathrm{A}$ to $\mathrm{A}^{+}$, while the cathode (right side) shows reduction of $\mathrm{B}^{2+}$ to $\mathrm{B}$.

The oxidation half-reaction is $\mathrm{A}_{(\mathrm{s})} \rightarrow \mathrm{A}^{+}_{(\mathrm{aq})} + \mathrme^{-}$, and the reduction half-reaction is $\mathrm{B}^{2+}_{(\mathrm{aq})} + 2\mathrme^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{B}_{(\mathrm{s})}$.

To balance electrons, multiply the oxidation half-reaction by 2: $2\mathrm{A}_{(\mathrm{s})} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{A}^{+}_{(\mathrm{aq})} + 2\mathrme^{-}$.

Combining both half-reactions gives $2\mathrm{A}_{(\mathrm{s})} + \mathrm{B}^{2+}_{(\mathrm{aq})} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{A}^{+}_{(\mathrm{aq})} + \mathrm{B}_{(\mathrm{s})}$, which matches option B.

Option A has incorrect stoichiometry, option C has reversed stoichiometry, and option D represents the reverse reaction.

The correct cell reaction is $\boxed{\text{B}}$.

57599.subject: Chemistry
57599.text: Which of the following compounds does not exhibit optical isomerism?
57599.sol:
Optical isomerism requires chirality, typically from a chiral carbon bonded to four distinct groups.

3-Iodohexane has a chiral carbon at position 3 bonded to -H, -I, -CH2CH3, and -CH2CH2CH3, so it exhibits optical isomerism.

2-Iodopentane has a chiral carbon at position 2 bonded to -H, -I, -CH3, and -CH2CH2CH3, so it exhibits optical isomerism.

2-Iodo-2-methylbutane has a carbon at position 2 bonded to -I, -CH3, another -CH3, and -CH2CH3. With two identical methyl groups, it is not chiral and does not exhibit optical isomerism.

2-Iodo-3-methylbutane has a chiral carbon at position 2 bonded to -H, -I, -CH3, and -CH(CH3)2, so it exhibits optical isomerism.

Thus, the compound that does not exhibit optical isomerism is $\boxed{C}$.

58407.subject: Chemistry
58407.text: What type of polymer the natural rubber is?
58407.sol:
Natural rubber is an addition polymer of isoprene (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene). It has weak intermolecular forces of attraction (van der Waals forces) between its polymer chains, which permit the polymer to be stretched. A few cross-links are introduced between the chains, which help the polymer retract to its original position after the force is released. Polymers with such elastic properties are classified as elastomers.

Therefore, natural rubber is an elastomer.

Answer: Elastomer

59164.subject: Chemistry
59164.text: Find the expected value of $\Delta \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{b}}$ for $1 \mathrm{ m} \mathrm{ Al Cl}_3$ solution in water if solution of nonelectrolyte of same concentration has $\Delta \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{b}}$ value ' $x$ ' K
59164.sol:
The elevation in boiling point for a $1\ \mathrm{m}$ nonelectrolyte solution is given as $x$ K, indicating the molal boiling point elevation constant is $K_\mathrm{b} = x$.

For $\mathrm{AlCl}_3$, which completely dissociates into $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$ and $3\ \mathrm{Cl}^-$ ions, the van't Hoff factor is $i = 4$.

The boiling point elevation for a $1\ \mathrm{m}\mathrm{AlCl}_3$ solution is then given by $\Delta T_\mathrm{b} = i \cdot K_\mathrm{b} \cdot m = 4 \cdot x \cdot 1 = 4x$ K.

The expected value is $\boxed{\text{D}}$.

59635.subject: Chemistry
59635.text:
The electronic configurations of elements are as-
$A = 1s^2 \ 2s^2 \ 2p^6 \ 3s^2 \ 3p^6 \ 4s^2$
$B = 1s^2 \ 2s^2 \ 2p^6 \ 3s^2 \ 3p^5$
Which of the following is formula of ionic compound that could be formed between these two elements A and B?
59635.sol:
Element A has the electronic configuration $1s^2 \ 2s^2 \ 2p^6 \ 3s^2 \ 3p^6 \ 4s^2$. It has $2$ valence electrons in its outermost shell, so it loses $2$ electrons to achieve a stable noble gas configuration, forming the $\textA^{2+}$ ion.

Element B has the electronic configuration $1s^2 \ 2s^2 \ 2p^6 \ 3s^2 \ 3p^5$. It has $7$ valence electrons in its outermost shell, so it gains $1$ electron to achieve a stable noble gas configuration, forming the $\textB^{-}$ ion.

To form a neutral ionic compound, one $\textA^{2+}$ ion combines with two $\textB^{-}$ ions.

The formula of the compound is $\text{AB}_2$.

Answer: $\text{AB}_2$

60718.subject: Mathematics
60718.text: The centre and radius of the circle $(a+1)x^2 + 3y^2 - 6x + 9y + a + 4 = 0$ are respectively...
60718.sol:
For the given equation to represent a circle, the coefficients of $x^2$ and $y^2$ must be equal.

$a + 1 = 3 \Rightarrow a = 2$

Substituting $a = 2$ into the given equation:

$3x^2 + 3y^2 - 6x + 9y + 6 = 0$

Dividing by $3$, we get the standard form of the circle:

$x^2 + y^2 - 2x + 3y + 2 = 0$

Comparing with $x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0$, we have $2g = -2$, $2f = 3$, and $c = 2$.

The centre of the circle is $(-g, -f) = \left(1, -\dfrac{3}{2}\right).

The radius of the circle is $ r = $\sqrt{g^2 + f^2 - c} = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + \left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^2 - 2} = \sqrt{1 + \dfrac{9}{4} - 2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{5}{4}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}.

Answer: \left(1, $-$\dfrac{3}{2}\right), \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$

61023.text: The value of the definite integral $\int_0^{\log_e 5}\dfrac{e^x\sqrt{e^x-1}}{e^x+3}\,dx$ is equal to...
61023.sol:
Let $e^x - 1 = t^2$, which gives $e^x dx = 2t dt$.

When $x = 0$, $t = 0$.

When $x = \log_e 5$, $t = 2$.

The integral becomes:

$I = \int_0^2 \dfrac{t}{t^2 + 1 + 3} (2t dt) = \int_0^2 \dfrac{2t^2}{t^2 + 4} dt$

$I = 2 \int_0^2 \dfrac{t^2 + 4 - 4}{t^2 + 4} dt$

$I = 2 \int_0^2 \left( 1 - \dfrac{4}{t^2 + 4} \right) dt$

$I = 2 \left[ t - 4 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \tan^{-1} \left( \dfrac{t}{2} \right) \right]_0^2

$I = 2 $\left[2 - 2 \tan^{-1}(1) \right]

$I = 2 $\left(2 - 2 \times \dfrac{\pi}{4} \right)

$I = 4 - \pi

Answer: 4 - \pi

62947.subject: Mathematics
62947.text:
Consider the statement patterns
A. $(q \rightarrow p) \vee (p \rightarrow q)$
B. $(\sim p \vee \sim q) \leftrightarrow \sim (p \wedge q)$
C. $[(p \vee q) \wedge \sim p] \wedge \sim q$
D. $(p \wedge q) \wedge (\sim p \vee \sim q)$
then statement patterns
options: A and B are contradictions, C and D are tautologies.
A and B are tautologies, C and D are contradictions.
A, B, C, D all are tautologies.
A, B, C, D all are contradictions.
62947.sol:
For statement pattern A:
$(q \rightarrow p) \vee (p \rightarrow q) \equiv (\sim q \vee p) \vee (\sim p \vee q) \equiv (\sim q \vee q) \vee (\sim p \vee p) \equiv T \vee T \equiv T$
Thus, A is a tautology.

For statement pattern B:
By De Morgan's Law, $\sim (p \wedge q) \equiv \sim p \vee \sim q$.
The statement becomes $(\sim p \vee \sim q) \leftrightarrow (\sim p \vee \sim q)$, which is of the form $X \leftrightarrow X \equiv T$.
Thus, B is a tautology.

For statement pattern C:
$[(p \vee q) \wedge \sim p] \wedge \sim q \equiv [(p \wedge \sim p) \vee (q \wedge \sim p)] \wedge \sim q \equiv [F \vee (q \wedge \sim p)] \wedge \sim q \equiv (q \wedge \sim p) \wedge \sim q \equiv \sim p \wedge (q \wedge \sim q) \equiv \sim p \wedge F \equiv F$
Thus, C is a contradiction.

For statement pattern D:
$(p \wedge q) \wedge (\sim p \vee \sim q) \equiv (p \wedge q) \wedge \sim (p \wedge q)$, which is of the form $X \wedge \sim X \equiv F$.
Thus, D is a contradiction.

Therefore, A and B are tautologies, while C and D are contradictions.

Answer: A and B are tautologies, C and D are contradictions.

65168.subject: Mathematics
65168.text: Let $\bar{a}=\hat{i}+\hat{\mathrm{j}}+\hat{\mathrm{k}}, \overline{\mathrm{b}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{c}}=\hat{\mathrm{j}}-\hat{\mathrm{k}}$ be three vectors such that $\bar{a} \times \overline{\mathrm{b}}=\overline{\mathrm{c}}$ and $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{c}=0$. If the length of projection vector of the vector $\overline{\mathrm{b}}$ on the vector $\bar{a} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}}$ is $l$, then the value of $3 l^2$ is
65168.sol:
Given vectors:

$\bar{a} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$

$\bar{c} = \hat{j} - \hat{k}$


The condition $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{c} = 0$ is satisfied since $\bar{a}$ and $\bar{c}$ are orthogonal.


Let $\bar{d} = \bar{a} \times \bar{c}$. Using the determinant form:

$\bar{d} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} \text{ and } \hat{j} \text{ and } \hat{k} \\ 1 \text{ and } 1 \text{ and } 1 \\ 0 \text{ and } 1 \text{ and } -1 \end{vmatrix} = -2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$


The magnitude is $|\bar{d}| = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + 1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{6}$.


The projection length of $\bar{b}$ on $\bar{d}$ is $l = \frac{|\bar{b} \cdot \bar{d}|}{|\bar{d}|}$.


Using the scalar triple product property:

$\bar{b} \cdot (\bar{a} \times \bar{c}) = -[\bar{a}\ \bar{b}\ \bar{c}] = -(\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) \cdot \bar{c}$


Given $\bar{a} \times \bar{b} = \bar{c}$, this becomes $-\bar{c} \cdot \bar{c} = -|\bar{c}|^2$.


Since $|\bar{c}|^2 = 1^2 + (-1)^2 = 2$, we have $\bar{b} \cdot \bar{d} = -2$.


The projection length is $l = \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}$ and $3l^2 = 3 \cdot \frac{4}{6} = 2$.


The final result is $2$.

65623.sol:
Resonance condition: Maximum current occurs when $X_L = X_C$, where $\omega L = \frac{1}{\omega C}$.

Angular frequency $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi(50) = 100\pi\ \text{rad/s}$.

Solving for capacitance: $C = \frac{1}{\omega^2 L} = \frac{1}{(100\pi)^2(2.5)}$.

Using $\pi^2 = 10$: $C = \frac{1}{10000 \cdot 10 \cdot 2.5} = \frac{1}{250000} = 4 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{F} = 4\ \mu\text{F}$.

At resonance, impedance equals resistance $Z = R = 11.5\ \Omega$, so peak current $I_0 = \frac{V_0}{R} = \frac{230}{11.5} = 20\ \text{A}$.

These values correspond to option B: $\boxed{\text{B}}$.

65882.text: The frequencies for series limit of Balmer and Paschen series are ' $v_1{ }^{\prime}$ and ' $v_3$ ' respectively. If frequency of first line of Balmer series ' $v_2$ ' then the relation between $v_1, v_2$ and $v_3$ is
65882.sol:
The frequencies of spectral lines in hydrogen are given by the Rydberg formula: $v = R c \left( \frac{1}{n_f^2} - \frac{1}{n_i^2} \right).

Series limit of Balmer series: $ n_i = $\infty to $ n_f = 2$, so $v_1 = $\frac{Rc}{4}.

First line of Balmer series: $ n_i = 3$ to $n_f = 2$, yielding $v_2 = $\frac{5Rc}{36}.

Series limit of Paschen series: $ n_i = $\infty to $ n_f = 3$, giving $v_3 = $\frac{Rc}{9}.

The energy difference $ E_\infty -$ E_2$ equals the sum $(E_\infty -$ E_3) + (E_3 - E_2)$. Dividing by Planck's constant $h$ gives $v_1 = v_3 + v_2$, or equivalently $v_1 - v_2 = v_3$.

Verifying numerically: \frac{Rc}{4} - \frac{5Rc}{36} = \frac{9Rc - 5Rc}{36} = \frac{4Rc}{36} = \frac{Rc}{9}, confirming $ v_1 - v_2 = v_3$.

The correct relationship is thus $v_1 - v_2 = v_3$, corresponding to option C.

66059.sol:
Analysis of circuit configuration: Capacitors $C_1$ and $C_2$ form a series combination, which is then connected in parallel with $C_3$ across voltage $V$.

The equivalent capacitance of the series combination is calculated as: $\frac{1}{C_{12}} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} = \frac{1}{C} + \frac{1}{2C} = \frac{3}{2C}$, giving $C_{12} = \frac{2C}{3}$.

The charge on $C_1$ equals the charge on the series combination: $Q_1 = C_{12}V = \frac{2CV}{3}$.

For $C_3$, directly connected across the battery: $Q_3 = C_3V = 3CV$.

The ratio is then: $\frac{Q_3}{Q_1} = \frac{3CV}{\frac{2CV}{3}} = \frac{9}{2}$.

Final result: $\frac{Q_3}{Q_1} = 4.5$

69740.text: Two spherical black bodies have radii ' $r_1$ ' and ' $r_2$ '. Their surface temperatures are ' $\mathrm{T}_1$ ' and ' $\mathrm{T}_2$ '. If they radiate same power, then $\frac{\mathrm{r}_2}{\mathrm{r}_1}$ is
69740.sol:
The power radiated by a spherical black body follows the Stefan-Boltzmann law: $P = e \sigma A T^4$. Since emissivity $e = 1$ for a black body and $A = 4\pi r^2$, the power becomes $P = \sigma (4\pi r^2) T^4$.

Given two spherical black bodies with radii $r_1$, $r_2$ and temperatures $T_1$, $T_2$ radiating equal power, equate their expressions:

$\sigma (4\pi r_1^2) T_1^4 = \sigma (4\pi r_2^2) T_2^4$

Canceling the common factors $\sigma$ and $4\pi$ yields:

$r_1^2 T_1^4 = r_2^2 T_2^4$

Rearranging for the radius ratio:

$\frac{r_2^2}{r_1^2} = \frac{T_1^4}{T_2^4}$

Taking square roots of both sides gives the final relationship:

$\frac{r_2}{r_1} = \left(\frac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^2$

This corresponds to option D.

70143.text: In Young's experiment, the intensity ratio of the maxima and minima in an interference pattern produced by two coherent sources is $36 : 1$. The ratio of the amplitudes of the two individual sources will be
70143.sol:
Let the amplitudes of the two sources be $A_1$ and $A_2$.

The maximum intensity $I_\max$ is proportional to $(A_1 + A_2)^2$ and the minimum intensity $I_\min$ is proportional to $(A_1 - A_2)^2$.

Given $\dfrac{I_\max}{I_\min} = \dfrac{36}{1}$

$\dfrac{(A_1 + A_2)^2}{(A_1 - A_2)^2} = \dfrac{36}{1}$

Taking the square root of both sides:

$\dfrac{A_1 + A_2}{A_1 - A_2} = \dfrac{6}{1}$

$A_1 + A_2 = 6A_1 - 6A_2$

$5A_1 = 7A_2$

$\dfrac{A_1}{A_2} = \dfrac{7}{5}$

The ratio of the amplitudes of the two individual sources is $7 : 5$.

Answer: $7 : 5$

70147.subject: Physics
70147.text:
In Young's double slit experiment, two slits are illuminated with a light of wavelength $\lambda$. The line joining $A_1P$ is perpendicular to $A_1A_2$ as shown in figure. If the first minimum is detected at P, the value of slits separation 'a' will be
(D = distance between source and screen)
70147.sol:
From the given figure, the path difference at point P is given by:

$\Delta x = A_2P - A_1P$

Using Pythagoras theorem in right-angled triangle $A_1A_2P$, we have $A_1P = D$ and $A_2P = \sqrt{D^2 + a^2}$.

So, $\Delta x = \sqrt{D^2 + a^2} - D$

For the first minimum to be detected at P, the path difference must be $\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$.

$\sqrt{D^2 + a^2} - D = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$

$\sqrt{D^2 + a^2} = D + \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$

Squaring both sides, we get:

$D^2 + a^2 = D^2 + D\lambda + \dfrac{\lambda^2}{4}$

$a^2 = D\lambda + \dfrac{\lambda^2}{4}$

Since the wavelength of light $\lambda$ is very small compared to the distance $D$ ($\lambda \ll D$), the term $\dfrac{\lambda^2}{4}$ is negligibly small and can be ignored.

$a^2 \approx D\lambda$

$a = \sqrt{\lambda D}$

Answer: $\sqrt{\lambda\text{D}}$

Minimum intensity $\propto(\text{ minimum amplitude })^2=16 x^2$
The ratio of the maximum to minimum intensity $=\frac{36}{16}=\frac{9}{4}$

71046.subject: Biology
71046.text:
Identify the correct sequence of processes in the decomposition of organic matter.
A. Humification
B. Fragmentation
C. Catabolism
D. Leaching
71046.sol:
Decomposition of organic matter involves the following steps in sequence:

Fragmentation: Breakdown of detritus into smaller particles by detritivores.

Leaching: Water-soluble inorganic nutrients seep into the soil horizon and precipitate as unavailable salts.

Catabolism: Degradation of detritus into simpler inorganic substances by bacterial and fungal enzymes.

Humification: Accumulation of a dark-coloured amorphous substance called humus.

Mineralisation: Further degradation of humus by microbes to release inorganic nutrients.

The correct sequence is Fragmentation \rightarrow Leaching \rightarrow Catabolism \rightarrow Humification, which corresponds to B \rightarrow D \rightarrow C \rightarrow A.

Answer: B \rightarrow D \rightarrow C \rightarrow A

71394.subject: Biology
71394.text: Which one of the following is NOT an example of complete sex linkage ?
71394.sol:
Complete sex linkage refers to the inheritance of genes located on the non-homologous regions of the X and Y chromosomes, which do not undergo crossing over. Examples of completely sex-linked traits in humans include red-green colour blindness, haemophilia, and myopia.

Incomplete sex linkage involves genes located on the homologous regions of the X and Y chromosomes, which can undergo crossing over. Examples of incompletely sex-linked traits include total colour blindness, retinitis pigmentosa, and nephritis.

Therefore, nephritis is an example of incomplete sex linkage, not complete sex linkage.

Answer: Nephritis

71744.subject: Chemistry
71744.text: Find the hybridization and number of coordinate bonds formed in tetracyanonickelate(II) ion respectively.
71744.sol:
The given complex ion is tetracyanonickelate(II), which is $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$.

The central metal ion is Ni in +2 oxidation state. The atomic number of Ni is 28, so the electronic configuration of $Ni^{2+}$ is $[Ar] 3d^8$.

Since $CN^-$ is a strong field ligand, it causes the pairing of the $3d$ electrons. The 8 electrons pair up to occupy four $3d$ orbitals, leaving one $3d$ orbital empty.

The empty orbitals available for hybridization are one $3d$, one $4s$, and two $4p$ orbitals. Thus, the hybridization is $dsp^2$, resulting in a square planar geometry.

Since there are four monodentate $CN^-$ ligands, each donates a pair of electrons to the central metal ion, forming a total of 4 coordinate bonds.

Therefore, the hybridization is $dsp^2$ and the number of coordinate bonds is 4.

Answer: $dsp^2$ and 4 coordinate bonds.

71810.text: Which among the following is false statement for enantiomers?
options: Enantiomers have equal but opposite optical rotation
Enantiomers are superimposable mirror images of each other.
71810.sol:
Enantiomers are stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other.

They have identical physical properties such as melting point, boiling point, and density.

They have the same chemical properties except when reacting with other chiral reagents.

They rotate the plane of polarized light by equal amounts but in opposite directions.

The statement that enantiomers are superimposable mirror images is false.

Answer: Enantiomers are superimposable mirror images of each other.

Equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to the direction of the electric field.

Since the electric field is along the Y-direction, the equipotential surfaces must be perpendicular to the Y-axis.

Planes perpendicular to the Y-axis are parallel to the XZ-plane.

The increasing magnitude of the electric field along the positive Y-direction implies that the spacing between consecutive equipotential surfaces decreases along this direction, but their orientation remains parallel to the XZ-plane.

Answer: planes parallel to XZ-plane.

76902.subject: Mathematics
76902.text: If $a$, $b$, $c$ are the sides of a triangle $ABC$ and $p$ is the perimeter of the triangle, then what is $\begin{vmatrix} p+c \text{ and } a \text{ and } b \\ c \text{ and } p+a \text{ and } b \\ c \text{ and } a \text{ and } p+b \end{vmatrix}$ equal to?
76902.sol:
Let $\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} p+c \text{ and } a \text{ and } b \\ c \text{ and } p+a \text{ and } b \\ c \text{ and } a \text{ and } p+b \end{vmatrix}$

Applying the column operation $C_1 \rightarrow C_1 + C_2 + C_3$:

$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} p+a+b+c \text{ and } a \text{ and } b \\ p+a+b+c \text{ and } p+a \text{ and } b \\ p+a+b+c \text{ and } a \text{ and } p+b \end{vmatrix}$

Since $p = a+b+c$ is the perimeter of the triangle, we have $p+a+b+c = 2p$. Substituting this into the determinant:

$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 2p \text{ and } a \text{ and } b \\ 2p \text{ and } p+a \text{ and } b \\ 2p \text{ and } a \text{ and } p+b \end{vmatrix}$

Taking $2p$ common from the first column $C_1$:

$\Delta = 2p \begin{vmatrix} 1 \text{ and } a \text{ and } b \\ 1 \text{ and } p+a \text{ and } b \\ 1 \text{ and } a \text{ and } p+b \end{vmatrix}$

Applying the row operations $R_2 \rightarrow R_2 - R_1$ and $R_3 \rightarrow R_3 - R_1$:

$\Delta = 2p \begin{vmatrix} 1 \text{ and } a \text{ and } b \\ 0 \text{ and } p \text{ and } 0 \\ 0 \text{ and } 0 \text{ and } p \end{vmatrix}$

Expanding the determinant along the first column $C_1$:

$\Delta = 2p [1(p \cdot p - 0)] = 2p(p^2) = 2p^3$

Answer: $2p^3$

Let \mathrm{a}=\mathrm{r} \sin \alpha, \mathrm{b}=\mathrm{r} \cos \alpha\begin{aligned}$& $\int \frac{d x}{r \sin \alpha \cos x+r \cos \alpha \sin x}=\frac{1}{r} \int \frac{1}{\sin (x+\alpha)}$\\

79647.text: Which one of the following statements is correct?
options: Both Azotobacter and Rhizobium fix atmospheric nitrogen in root nodules of plants.
Cyanobacteria such as Anabaena and Nostoc are important mobilizers of phosphates and for plant nutrition in soil
At present it is not possible to grow maize without chemical fertilizers

79647.sol:
Rhizobium fix nitrogen in root nodules of legumes, while Azotobacter is a free-living nitrogen-fixing bacterium. Anabaena and Nostoc are not mobilisers of phosphates. Anabaena is a filamentous cyanobacteria, involved in nitrogen fixation. Extensive use of chemical fertilizers may lead to eutrophication of nearby waterbodies.
Related Theory
Eutrophication or more precisely hypertrophication, refers to enrichment of $a$ water body with nutrients, usually with an excess amount of nutrients. This process induces growth of plants and algae and, due to the biomass load, may result in oxygen depletion of the water body. For example, algal bloom.

79928.subject: Botany
options: The establishment of a new biotic community is very fast in its primary phase.
The numbers and types of animals remain constant.
The changes lead to a community that is in near equilibrium with the environment and is called pioneer community.
The gradual and predictable change in species composition occurs in a given area.
79928.sol:
Ecological succession involves a gradual and fairly predictable change in the species composition of a given area, i.e., the numbers and types of animals. The establishment of a new biotic community is very slow in its primary phase.

The first set of species or community that develops in a bare area in ecological succession is the pioneer community. Pioneer species facilitate succession. The final steady stable self-sustaining community in an ecological succession that lead to a community that is in near equilibrium with the environment and is called climax community.

80221.subject: Botany
80221.text: In leaves of $\mathrm{C}_4$-plants malic acid synthesis during $\mathrm{CO}_2$-fixation occurs in
80221.sol:
$\mathrm{C}_4$-plants show Kranz anatomy. In the leaves of $\mathrm{C}_4$-plants the vascular bundles are surrounded by bundle sheath of parenchymatous cells, which in turn are surrounded by mesophyll cells. In $\mathrm{C}_4$-plants the Hatch and Slack pathway involves two carboxylation reaction one taking place in chloroplast of mesophyll cells and other in chloroplast of bundle sheath cells. The initial $\mathrm{CO}_2$ fixation occurs in mesophyll cells where primary $\mathrm{CO}_2$ acceptor is phosphoenol pyruvate and formed oxaloacetate. The oxaloacetate is reduced to malic acid. From chloroplasts of mesophyll cells the malic acid is transferred to chloroplast of bundle sheath cells and decarboxylated to form $\mathrm{CO}_2$ and pyruvic acid. The $\mathrm{CO}_2$ is again fixed by $\mathrm{C}_3$ cycle.
In plants, stoma is surrounded by two small, specialized, green epidermal cells called guard cells. The guard cells are small in size and therefore, rapidly influenced by turgor changes.

82044.subject: Chemistry
82044.text:
Two moles of an ideal gas undergo free expansion from $10$ L to $100$ L at $300$ K. The values of $\Delta S_{\text{system}}$ and $\Delta S_{\text{surroundings}}$ are
(R is universal gas constant)
82044.sol:
For the free expansion of an ideal gas, the external pressure is zero, so the work done $W = 0$.

Since the process is isothermal at $300$ K, the change in internal energy $\Delta U = 0$.

From the first law of thermodynamics, $q = \Delta U - W = 0$.

Since no heat is exchanged with the surroundings, the change in entropy of the surroundings is:

$\Delta S_{\text{surroundings}} = \dfrac{q_{\text{surr}}}{T} = 0$

Entropy is a state function, so the change in entropy of the system for an isothermal expansion is calculated using a reversible path between the same initial and final states:

$\Delta S_{\text{system}} = nR \ln\left(\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}\right)$

Substituting $n = 2$ moles, $V_1 = 10$ L, and $V_2 = 100$ L:

$\Delta S_{\text{system}} = 2R \ln\left(\dfrac{100}{10}\right) = 2R \ln(10)$

Using $\ln(10) = 2.303 \log_{10}(10) = 2.303$:

$\Delta S_{\text{system}} = 2 \times 2.303 R = 4.606 R$

Answer: $\Delta S_{\text{system}}=4.606$ R; $\Delta S_{\text{surroundings}}=0$

82770.subject: Physics
82770.text: Assuming that the gravitational potential energy of an object at infinity is zero, the change in potential energy (final - initial) of an object of mass $m$, when taken to a height $\mathrm{h}$ from the surface of earth (of radius $\mathrm{R}$ ) is given by,
82770.sol:
The gravitational potential energy of an object placed at earth's surface is
$$
\mathrm{U}_1=-\frac{\mathrm{GMm}}{\mathrm{R}}
$$
where, $G=$ gravitational constant,
$M=$ Mass of earth, $m=$ mass of object and
$\mathrm{R}=$ radius of the earth
The negative sign in the above relation indicates that it is the work done in bringing the object from infinity to a distance $R$.
The gravitational potential energy of object at a height habove the surface of earth is
$$
\mathrm{U}_2=-\frac{\mathrm{GMm}}{(\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{h})}
$$
So, the change in potential energy is
$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta U & =\mathrm{U}_2-\mathrm{U}_1=-\frac{\mathrm{GMm}}{\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{h}}-\left(-\frac{\mathrm{GMm}}{\mathrm{R}}\right) \\

options: Mathew Meselson and F. Stahl - Pisum sativum
Alfred Harshey and Martha Chase - TMV
Francois Jacob and Jacques Monod - Lac operon
84924.sol:
Francois Jacob (a geneticist) and Jacques Monod (a biochemist) proposed a model of gene regulation, known as operon model in bacteria in 1961. Operon is a co-ordinate group of genes such as structural gene, operator gene, promoter gene, regulator gene which function together and regulate a metabolic pathway as a unit, e.g., lac operon, trp operon, ara operon, his operon, val operon etc.

Matthew Meselson and F. Stahl discovered the semi-conservative model of DNA replication in E. coli. Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase use T2 bacteriophage in their experiments to infect E. coli and proved that DNA is the genetic material. Alec Jeffreys (1984) invented the DNA fingerprinting technique. This technique determines nucleotide sequences of certain areas of DNA which are unique to each individual.

86511.subject: Mathematics
86511.text: The probability that the sum of two integers $m$ and $n$, where $m, n \in \{1, 2, \ldots, 50\}$, chosen randomly and independently, being divisible by $3$ is
86511.sol:
Let the given set of $50$ integers be partitioned into three subsets $S_0, S_1, S_2$ based on the remainder when divided by $3$.

The number of elements in these subsets are $n(S_0) = 16$ (multiples of $3$), $n(S_1) = 17$ (leaving remainder $1$), and $n(S_2) = 17$ (leaving remainder $2$).

For the sum $m+n$ to be a multiple of $3$, the pair $(m, n)$ must be selected from $(S_0, S_0)$, $(S_1, S_2)$, or $(S_2, S_1)$.

The number of favorable ways to choose the pair $(m, n)$ is $16 \times 16 + 17 \times 17 + 17 \times 17 = 256 + 289 + 289 = 834$.

Since $m$ and $n$ are chosen independently, the total number of ways to choose the pair is $50 \times 50 = 2500$.

The probability is $\dfrac{834}{2500} = \dfrac{834 \times 4}{2500 \times 4} = \dfrac{3336}{10000} = 0.3336$.

101589.subject: Physics
101589.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R

Assertion A: When you squeeze one end of a tube to get toothpaste out from the other end, Pascal’s principle is observed.

Reason R: A change in the pressure applied to an enclosed incompressible fluid is transmitted undiminished to every portion of the fluid and to the walls of its container.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
options: Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is not correct but R is correct
A is correct but R is not correct
Both A and R is correct and R is the correct explanation of A
101589.sol:
Pascal's law states that the pressure in a closed incompressible fluid is transmitted equally in all directions.

The formula for pressure is given by

$P = \dfrac{F}{A}$

When a toothpaste is squeezed let the pressure transmitted by $P$. At the mouth of the toothpaste the pressure will also be equal to $P$ due to Pascal's law. The pressure applied to the tube is transmitted equally throughout the toothpaste. When the pressure reaches the open end, it forces toothpaste out through the opening. Hence, both $A \text{ and } R$ is correct and $R$ is correct explanation for  $A$.

102939.subject: Physics
102939.text: The electric field $E$ due to a charged spherical object of radius $R$ is found to be zero for $r < R$ and proportional to $\dfrac{1}{r^2}$ for $r > R$ (where $r$ is the distance from the centre of the object). Which of the following objects could produce this electric field profile?
options: A uniformly charged solid non-conducting sphere only
A uniformly charged hollow conducting sphere only
A uniformly charged solid conducting sphere only
Either a uniformly charged solid conducting sphere or a uniformly charged hollow conducting sphere
102939.sol:
For $r < R$, the electric field is zero. This indicates that there is no charge enclosed within any radius $r < R$.

For $r > R$, the electric field is proportional to $\dfrac{1}{r^2}$, which is characteristic of a spherical charge distribution where the entire charge can be assumed to be concentrated at the centre.

In both a hollow conducting sphere and a solid conducting sphere, any excess charge resides entirely on the outer surface. Therefore, the electric field inside ($r < R$) is zero, and outside ($r > R$) it follows the inverse-square law.

In contrast, a uniformly charged solid non-conducting sphere has charge distributed throughout its volume, so its internal electric field is non-zero and proportional to $r$. Thus, the given profile can be produced by either a solid or a hollow conducting sphere.

Answer: Either a uniformly charged solid conducting sphere or a uniformly charged hollow conducting sphere

104468.subject: Physics
104468.text: A light ray is incident normally on one of the mutually perpendicular faces of a right-angled thin prism. The refractive index of the material of the prism is $1.6$. If the ray emerges from the inclined face at an angle of $8^{\circ}$ with respect to the normal of that face, the angle of the prism is
104468.sol:
For normal incidence on the first face, the angle of incidence $i_{1} = 0^{\circ}$, which implies the angle of refraction $r_{1} = 0^{\circ}$.

For a prism, the angle of the prism $A = r_{1} + r_{2}$. Therefore, the angle of incidence at the second face is $r_{2} = A$.

Applying Snell's law at the second face (from prism to air) and using the small angle approximation for a thin prism:
$\mu \times r_{2} = 1 \times e$
$\mu \times A = e$

Substituting the given values ($\mu = 1.6$ and $e = 8^{\circ}$):
$1.6 \times A = 8^{\circ}$
$A = \dfrac{8^{\circ}}{1.6} = 5^{\circ}$

Answer: $5^{\circ}$

104476.subject: Physics
104476.text: An amateur astronomer designs an astronomical telescope in normal adjustment. The total tube length of the telescope is $105 \mathrm{~cm}$ and its magnifying power has a magnitude of $20$. What are the optical powers of the objective and the eyepiece lenses respectively?
104476.sol:
For an astronomical telescope in normal adjustment, the magnitude of magnifying power is given by:
$|m| = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e} = 20 \Rightarrow f_o = 20 f_e$

The tube length is given by:
$L = f_o + f_e = 105 \mathrm{~cm}$

Substituting $f_o$:
$20 f_e + f_e = 105 \mathrm{~cm}$
$21 f_e = 105 \mathrm{~cm} \Rightarrow f_e = 5 \mathrm{~cm} = 0.05 \mathrm{~m}$

Then, the focal length of the objective is:
$f_o = 20 \times 5 = 100 \mathrm{~cm} = 1 \mathrm{~m}$

The optical power of a lens is $P = \dfrac{1}{f(\text{in meters})}$.

Power of the objective:
$P_o = \dfrac{1}{1} = +1 \mathrm{~D}$

Power of the eyepiece:
$P_e = \dfrac{1}{0.05} = +20 \mathrm{~D}$

Therefore, the powers of the objective and eyepiece are $+1 \mathrm{~D}$ and $+20 \mathrm{~D}$ respectively.

Answer: $+1 \mathrm{~D}$ and $+20 \mathrm{~D}$

106450.subject: Chemistry
106450.text: For a particular subshell, the total number of permissible values of the magnetic quantum number is 7. If the number of radial nodes for this subshell is 2, the correct designation of the subshell is:
106450.sol:
The total number of permissible values of the magnetic quantum number for a subshell is given by $2l + 1$.

Given that $2l + 1 = 7$, we find $2l = 6 \Rightarrow l = 3$. An azimuthal quantum number of $l = 3$ corresponds to an $f$ subshell.

The formula for the number of radial nodes is $n - l - 1$.

Given that the number of radial nodes is 2, we can substitute $l = 3$ into the formula:
$n - 3 - 1 = 2$
$n - 4 = 2 \Rightarrow n = 6$

Therefore, the principal quantum number is $n = 6$ and the subshell is $6f$.

Option 1 is incorrect because it corresponds to $n-l = 2$ instead of $n-l-1 = 2$. Option 4 is incorrect because it assumes $l=2$ (a $d$ subshell) due to an arithmetic error.

Answer: $6f$

Reason (R): The highest occupied molecular orbital in $\mathrm{B}_2$ is a $\sigma 2\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{z}$ orbital containing two unpaired electrons.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
options: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.
107760.sol:
The total number of electrons in a $\mathrm{B}_2$ molecule is 10.

For molecules with up to 14 electrons, the molecular orbital energy level sequence is:
$\sigma 1\mathrm{s} < \sigma^{*} 1\mathrm{s} < \sigma 2\mathrm{s} < \sigma^{*} 2\mathrm{s} < (\pi 2\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{x} = \pi 2\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{y}) < \sigma 2\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{z} < (\pi^{*} 2\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{x} = \pi^{*} 2\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{y}) < \sigma^{*} 2\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{z}$

Filling the 10 electrons, the electronic configuration of $\mathrm{B}_2$ is:
$\sigma 1\mathrm{s}^2, \sigma^{*} 1\mathrm{s}^2, \sigma 2\mathrm{s}^2, \sigma^{*} 2\mathrm{s}^2, \pi 2\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{x}^1 = \pi 2\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{y}^1$

Since there are two unpaired electrons in the degenerate $\pi 2\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{x}$ and $\pi 2\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{y}$ orbitals, $\mathrm{B}_2$ is paramagnetic. Thus, Assertion (A) is true.

The highest occupied molecular orbitals are $\pi 2\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{x}$ and $\pi 2\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{y}$, not $\sigma 2\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{z}$. Thus, Reason (R) is false.

Answer: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

108652.subject: Chemistry
108652.text: An ideal gas undergoes a thermodynamic process from state A to state B. The process is represented on a pressure-volume (P-V) diagram as a curve where pressure is inversely proportional to volume ($P \propto \dfrac{1}{V}$). Which of the following is correct for the changes in internal energy ($\Delta U$) and enthalpy ($\Delta H$) of the gas during this process?
108652.sol:
For an ideal gas, the condition $P \propto \dfrac{1}{V}$ implies that $PV = \text{constant}$.

According to the ideal gas equation, $PV = nRT$. If $PV$ is constant, the temperature $T$ must be constant, meaning the process is isothermal ($\Delta T = 0$).

For an ideal gas, both internal energy ($U$) and enthalpy ($H$) are functions of temperature only. Since there is no change in temperature, the change in internal energy ($\Delta U$) and the change in enthalpy ($\Delta H$) are both zero.

Therefore, $\Delta U = 0$ and $\Delta H = 0$.

Answer: $\Delta U = 0$, $\Delta H = 0$

109386.subject: Chemistry
109386.text: At $298$ K, an acidic buffer solution containing a weak acid $HY$ and its salt $NaY$ has a pH of $5$. If the base dissociation constant ($K_b$) for the conjugate base $Y^{-}$ is $10^{-10}$, what is the ratio of the concentration of $Y^{-}$ to $HY$ in the buffer?
109386.sol:
Given $K_b$ for the conjugate base $Y^{-} = 10^{-10}$.

For a conjugate acid-base pair at $298$ K, $K_a \times K_b = K_w = 10^{-14}$.

$K_a = \dfrac{10^{-14}}{10^{-10}} = 10^{-4}$

The $pK_a$ of the weak acid $HY$ is:

$pK_a = -\log(K_a) = -\log(10^{-4}) = 4$

Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for an acidic buffer:

$\text{pH} = pK_a + \log \left( \dfrac{[Y^{-}]}{[HY]} \right)$

Substitute the given values ($\text{pH} = 5$):

$5 = 4 + \log \left( \dfrac{[Y^{-}]}{[HY]} \right)$

$\log \left( \dfrac{[Y^{-}]}{[HY]} \right) = 1$

Taking the antilogarithm on both sides:

$\dfrac{[Y^{-}]}{[HY]} = 10^1 = 10$

Thus, the ratio of the concentration of $Y^{-}$ to $HY$ is $10 : 1$.

Answer: $10 : 1$

113957.text: A mixture of two miscible liquids $A$ and $B$ is distilled under equilibrium conditions at $1 \mathrm{~atm}$ pressure. The mole fraction of $A$ in solution and vapour phase are 0.30 and 0.60 respectively. Assuming ideal behaviour of the solution and the vapour, calculate the ratio of the vapour pressure of pure $A$ to that of pure $B$
113957.sol:
In solution, $x_A=0.30 ; x_B=0.70$
In vapour phase, $x_A^{\prime}=0.60 ; x_B^{\prime}=0.40$
Using Dalton's law and Raoult's law
$\begin{aligned} & x_A^{\prime}=0.60=\frac{p_A}{P}=\frac{p_A}{p_A+p_B}=\frac{0.30 p_A^{\circ}}{0.30 p_A^{\circ}+0.70 p_B^{\circ}} \\ & x_B^{\prime}=0.40=\frac{p_B}{P}=\frac{p_B}{p_A+p_B}=\frac{0.70 p_B^{\circ}}{0.30 p_A^{\circ}+0.70 p_B^{\circ}} \\ & \frac{x_A^{\prime}}{x_B^{\prime}}=\frac{0.60}{0.40}=\frac{0.30 p_A^{\circ}}{0.70 p_B^{\circ}} \\ & \frac{p_A^{\circ}}{p_B^{\circ}}=\frac{0.60 \times 0.70}{0.40 \times 0.30}=\frac{7}{2}=3.5\end{aligned}$

114385.subject: Chemistry
114385.text:
Calculate the emf of the following galvanic cell at $298\text{ K}$:

$\text{Cu(s)} + 2\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{Ag(s)}$

Given: $E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 0.46\text{ V}$, $[\text{Cu}^{2+}] = 0.1\text{ M}$, $[\text{Ag}^{+}] = 0.01\text{ M}$, and $\dfrac{2.303\text{ RT}}{\text{F}} = 0.059\text{ V}$ at $298\text{ K}$.
114385.sol:
The given cell reaction is:
$\text{Cu(s)} + 2\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{Ag(s)}$

The number of electrons transferred, $n = 2$.

According to the Nernst equation:
$E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0.059}{n} \log \dfrac{[\text{Cu}^{2+}]}{[\text{Ag}^{+}]^{2}}$

Substituting the given values:
$E_{\text{cell}} = 0.46 - \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log \dfrac{0.1}{(0.01)^{2}}$

$E_{\text{cell}} = 0.46 - 0.0295 \log \dfrac{0.1}{10^{-4}}$

$E_{\text{cell}} = 0.46 - 0.0295 \log (10^{3})$

$E_{\text{cell}} = 0.46 - 0.0295 \times 3$

$E_{\text{cell}} = 0.46 - 0.0885 = 0.3715\text{ V}$

If $[\text{Ag}^{+}]$ is not squared in the reaction quotient, it leads to the incorrect value of $0.4305\text{ V}$.

Answer: $0.3715\text{ V}$

119268.subject: Chemistry
119268.text:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the total number of structurally distinct aldol condensation products (including both self and cross products, but excluding stereoisomers) formed when the given pairs of carbonyl compounds are heated with dilute $\text{NaOH}$.

List-I (Reactants)List-II (Total products)
(A) Ethanal + Propanal(I) 0
(B) Propanone + Pentan-2-one(II) 2
(C) Benzaldehyde + Acetophenone(III) 4
(D) Formaldehyde + Benzophenone(IV) 6

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
119268.sol:
The number of aldol products depends on the number of distinct enolates that can form and the number of electrophilic carbonyl carbons available.

(A) Ethanal has 1 type of $\alpha$-hydrogen and Propanal has 1 type. Total products = 1 (self-ethanal) + 1 (self-propanal) + 2 (cross) = 4.

(B) Propanone has 1 type of $\alpha$-hydrogen. Pentan-2-one has 2 types of $\alpha$-hydrogens ($\text{C}_1$ and $\text{C}_3$), thus forming two different enolates. Total products = 1 (self-propanone) + 2 (self-pentan-2-one) + 3 (cross products: propanone enolate with pentan-2-one, and two pentan-2-one enolates with propanone) = 6.

(C) Benzaldehyde has no $\alpha$-hydrogen, while Acetophenone has 1 type. Total products = 1 (self-acetophenone) + 1 (cross: acetophenone enolate with benzaldehyde) = 2.

(D) Both Formaldehyde and Benzophenone lack $\alpha$-hydrogens, so no aldol condensation can occur. Total products = 0.

Therefore, the correct match is (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I).

Answer: (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)

123221.subject: Botany
123221.sol: The outermost layer is epiblema. Many of the cells of epiblema protrude in the form of unicellular root hairs. The cortex consists of several layers of thin-walled parenchyma cells with intercellular spaces. The innermost layer of the cortex is called endodermis. It comprises a single layer of barrel-shaped cells without any intercellular spaces. The tangential as well as radial walls of the endodermal cells have a deposition of water-impermeable, waxy material suberin in the form of casparian strips. Next to endodermis lies a few layers of thick-walled parenchyomatous cells referred to as pericycle. Initiation of lateral roots and vascular cambium during the secondary growth takes place in these cells. The pith is small or inconspicuous.The parenchymatous cells which lie between the xylem and the phloem are called conjuctive tissue. There are usually two to four xylem and phloem patches. Later, a cambium ring develops between the xylem and phloem. All tissues on the innerside of the endodermis such as pericycle, vascular bundles and pith constitute the stele.

123641.subject: Botany
123641.text: What are the daughter cells produced by mitosis?
123641.sol: Mitosis usually results in the production of diploid daughter cells with identical genetic complement. Cell growth results in disturbing the ratio between the nucleus and the cytoplasm. It therefore becomes essential for the cell to divide to restore the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio. A very significant contribution of mitosis is cell repair. The cells of the upper layer of the epidermis, cells of the lining of the gut, and blood cells are being constantly replaced. Mitotic divisions in the meristematic tissues – the apical and the lateral cambium, result in a continuous growth of plants throughout their life.

124031.subject: Botany
124031.text: What is the function of food vacuoles in cells?
options: To store water and other materials
To transport ions and other materials against concentration gradients into the vacuole
To regulate osmotic pressure and excretion
124031.sol: The vacuole is the membrane-bound space found in the cytoplasm. It contains water, sap, excretory product and other materials not useful for the cell. The vacuole is bound by a single membrane called tonoplast. In plant cells the vacuoles can occupy up to 90 per cent of the volume of the cell. In plants, the tonoplast facilitates the transport of a number of ions and other materials against concentration gradients into the vacuole, hence their concentration is significantly higher in the vacuole than in the cytoplasm. In Amoeba the contractile vacuole is important for osmoregulation and excretion. In many cells, as in protists, food vacuoles are formed by engulfing the food particles..
